architecture.mechanism: The helical coil is treated as a self-supporting structural spring whose pitch stability comes from elastic preload and distributed mechanical constraint, not from metallurgical bonding; scale deposition is reduced by maintaining a continuous thin-film flow regime and by making the coil surface energetically unfavorable to calcium carbonate nucleation.
architecture.intervention: Wind the copper tube on a mandrel with a controlled axial preload so the coil is slightly compressed against the cylindrical shroud inner wall, then install a removable slotted pitch-retention cage (stainless steel or PEEK) that engages each coil turn at three or more circumferential points without soldering; apply a thin hydrophobic or low-surface-energy coating (e.g., PTFE or silane-based) to the coil exterior and shroud interior to reduce scale adhesion, and add a short straight inlet diffuser to stabilize flow before the helical section.
architecture.expected_effect: Coil pitch remains within ±2% of nominal after 500 daily descaling cycles and repeated thermal expansion; scale mass accumulation on the coil surface is reduced by at least 50% compared to bare copper under identical water hardness and descaling schedule; pressure drop across the module changes by less than 10% over the same period.
architecture.falsification_test: Build one prototype with the pitch-retention cage and one bare soldered-free coil, run both through 100 accelerated descaling cycles (citric or lactic acid at 60–80°C) with hard water (e.g., 300 ppm CaCO3 equivalent), and measure pitch deviation and scale mass; if the caged coil shows no significant improvement in pitch stability or scale reduction, the architecture is rejected.
